steps.label: Turn the sum into a product
steps.margin_note: First mark. cos66° = sin24°, then sin p + sin q = 2 sin((p+q)/2) cos((p−q)/2) with C = 84° and D = 24°, giving half sum 54° and half difference 30°.
steps.memory_tip: Turn cos66° into sin24° first, then use sin p + sin q = 2 sin((p+q)/2) cos((p−q)/2).
lines: [∵ sin p + sin q = 2 sin((p+q)/2) cos((p−q)/2)]

recall.must_convey: That cos66° = sin24°, and the sum to product formula gives 8 sin54° cos30°.
accept: cos sixty six is sin twenty four
use sin C plus sin D equals two sin of half the sum cos of half the difference
the half sum is fifty four and the half difference is thirty
cos sixty six ante sin twenty four, appudu sum to product apply chestham
it becomes eight sin fifty four cos thirty

steps.why: Once cos66° is written as sin24° both terms are sines, so the sum to product formula applies. The half sum 54° and half difference 30° are both angles with exact values.
common_mistakes: Swapping the half sum and the half difference.

steps.label: Put in the exact values
steps.margin_note: Second mark. cos30° = √3/2 and sin54° = cos36° = (√5 + 1)/4. The 4 in that value cancels the 4 outside.
steps.memory_tip: sin54° = cos36° = (√5 + 1)/4, and its 4 cancels the 4 standing in front.

recall.must_convey: That cos30° = √3/2 and sin54° = cos36° = (√5 + 1)/4 are substituted, giving √15 + √3.
accept: cos thirty is root three by two and sin fifty four is cos thirty six
cos thirty six is root five plus one over four
the four cancels and root three times root five plus one is root fifteen plus root three
sin fifty four ante cos thirty six, value root five plus one by four
the answer is root fifteen plus root three

steps.why: 54° and 36° are complementary, so sin54° is the standard value cos36°. Multiplying √3 into the bracket gives √15 from √3 × √5.
